learningObjectives.title: Reactivity 3.1 Proton transfer reactions (acids and bases)

questions.q: A Bronsted-Lowry acid is defined as a:
questions.explain: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton; a base accepts one.

questions.q: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a:
questions.explain: Bases accept protons; for example, ammonia accepts H+ to form NH4+.

questions.q: In the reaction HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl-, water acts as a:
questions.explain: Water accepts a proton from HCl, forming the hydronium ion H3O+.

questions.q: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by:
questions.explain: The conjugate base is what remains after an acid loses a proton (e.g. HCl/Cl-).

questions.q: A strong acid is one that:
questions.explain: Strong acids such as HCl dissociate completely; weak acids only partially.

questions.q: A weak base such as ammonia:
questions.explain: Weak bases establish an equilibrium, accepting protons only partially.

questions.q: On the pH scale, a neutral solution at 25 degrees C has a pH of:
questions.explain: At 25 degrees C, neutral pH is 7; acids are below 7 and bases above 7.

questions.q: A solution with pH 2 is:
questions.explain: Low pH values indicate high hydrogen-ion concentration and strong acidity.

questions.q: As pH increases from 3 to 6, the hydrogen ion concentration:
questions.explain: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H+]; three units is 10^3 = 1000 times lower.

questions.q: The reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate produces:
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO2 (which turns limewater milky).

questions.q: The reaction of an acid with a reactive metal produces:
questions.explain: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen (which gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint).

questions.q: The reaction of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide produces:
questions.explain: Acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation): HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O.

questions.q: In neutralisation, the ionic equation common to strong acid and strong alkali reactions is:
questions.explain: The net ionic reaction is the combination of hydrogen and hydroxide ions to form water.

questions.q: Which is the conjugate base of the acid HNO3?
questions.explain: Removing a proton from HNO3 gives its conjugate base, NO3-.

questions.q: Which is the conjugate acid of the base NH3?
questions.explain: Adding a proton to ammonia gives the ammonium ion NH4+.

questions.q: Compared with a strong acid of the same concentration, a weak acid has:
questions.explain: A weak acid ionises less, giving a lower [H+] and therefore a higher pH.

questions.q: An indicator used to distinguish acids and bases changes:
questions.explain: Indicators such as litmus or universal indicator change colour with pH.

questions.q: Litmus paper in an alkaline solution turns:
questions.explain: Litmus is blue in alkali and red in acid.

questions.q: A species that can act as both an acid and a base (like water) is described as:
questions.explain: Water can donate or accept a proton, so it is amphiprotic.

questions.q: Reacting an acid with a metal oxide (a base) produces:
questions.explain: Acid + metal oxide → salt + water (a neutralisation).
